mainTopic: The end of the אונקלוס story and the destructions of ירושלים, טור מלכא, כפר סכניא and ביתר
overview: This amud finishes the story of אונקלוס, who raises טיטוס, בלעם and ישו from the dead. Each one says Israel is most important in the next world, and each is punished in a way that fits his sin. רבי אלעזר then closes the story of בר קמצא with a lesson: shame is so powerful that it led to the חורבן. Next the גמרא tells how טור מלכא was destroyed. A fight over a rooster and a hen was reported to the קיסר as a revolt. The hero בר דרומא fell because of his own words, and the Jews' celebration brought the Romans back. The גמרא describes how huge הר המלך once was and explains, with the image of a deer's skin, how ארץ ישראל can have held so many people. Three stories about the righteous town of כפר סכניא follow, and רב יוסף explains that it was punished for not mourning ירושלים. Finally, a cedar cut down for a broken carriage pole leads to the destruction of ביתר, where the bloodshed was enormous.

steps.title: טיטוס describes his own punishment
steps.stepSummary: טיטוס finishes answering אונקלוס: his punishment is the very thing he asked for. Every day his ashes are gathered, he is judged, burned, and scattered over the seven seas.
steps.simpleTranslation: His punishment is what he decreed on himself: every day they gather his ashes and judge him, then they burn him and scatter him over the seven seas.
steps.whatsHappening: טיטוס is finishing his answer to אונקלוס's question about how he is punished in the next world.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טיטוס had asked that his body be burned and scattered so God could not find him to judge him. The punishment turns his own plan against him: the burning and scattering happen to him again every single day, and he is judged anyway.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sets the pattern for the whole section: each figure's punishment in the next world fits the sin he did in this world (מידה כנגד מידה).

phrases.english: With what he decreed upon himself –
phrases.notes: He means טיטוס, who asked earlier in the story that his ashes be scattered so that God could not judge him.

phrases.english: every day they gather his ashes
and they judge him, and they burn him
and they scatter him over the seven seas.
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in square brackets; it belongs to the corrected wording.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the טיטוס conversation that began before this section.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: טיטוס is burned, judged, and scattered over the seven seas every day.

steps.title: אונקלוס raises בלעם and asks whether to join Israel
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס raises בלעם from the dead and asks who is most important in the next world. בלעם says Israel. When asked whether to join them, בלעם answers with a פסוק: do not seek their peace or their welfare.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and raised בלעם through necromancy. He asked him: Who is important in that world? He said: Israel. Should I join them? He answered: 'Do not seek their peace or their good all your days.'
steps.whatsHappening: אונקלוס moves to a second figure, בלעם, and asks him the same questions he asked טיטוס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם admits that Israel is the most important nation in the next world, yet he still tells אונקלוס not to help them. He turns a פסוק about עמון and מואב into advice against Israel, which shows how deep his hatred is.

keyTerms.meaning: he brought him up (from the grave)

phrases.english: He went and raised Balaam through necromancy,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאן חֲשִׁיב בְּהָהוּא עָלְמָא?
phrases.english: He said to him: Who is important in that world?
He said to him: Israel.
Should I attach myself to them?
He said to him: "You shall not seek their peace
phrases.notes: דברים 23:7

phrases.english: or their welfare all the days."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same questions as with טיטוס, now asked of a new figure.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who is important in the next world, and should אונקלוס join them?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Israel is most important, but do not seek their peace or welfare.

steps.title: בלעם's punishment
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס asks בלעם what his own punishment is. בלעם answers that he is punished in boiling semen.
steps.simpleTranslation: He asked him: What is the punishment of 'that man'? He said: In boiling semen.
steps.whatsHappening: אונקלוס asks בלעם about his own punishment, and בלעם describes it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Again the punishment fits the sin. בלעם gave the advice that caused Israel to sin with the daughters of מואב, so his punishment matches that kind of sin.

keyTerms.meaning: 'that man', a polite way to say 'you yourself'

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּינֵיהּ דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא בְּמַאי?
phrases.english: He said to him: The judgment of that man, with what is it?
phrases.notes: 'That man' is a polite way of saying 'you'. He is asking בלעם about his own punishment.

phrases.english: He said to him: With boiling semen.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּינֵיהּ דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא בְּמַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same conversation with בלעם, now asking about his punishment.

steps.title: אונקלוס raises ישו and asks whether to join Israel
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס raises ישו הנוצרי and asks the same questions. He also says Israel is most important, but advises the opposite of בלעם: seek their good, not their harm, because touching them is like touching the apple of God's eye.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went and raised ישו הנוצרי through necromancy. He asked: Who is important in that world? He said: Israel. Should I join them? He said: Seek their good, do not seek their harm. Whoever touches them is as if he touches the apple of His eye.
steps.whatsHappening: אונקלוס asks a third figure the same questions, and this time gets advice that favors Israel.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both בלעם and ישו agree that Israel is most important in the next world. The difference is in the advice: בלעם says not to seek their good, while ישו says to seek their good and warns that harming them is like harming God's most precious possession.

phrases.english: He went and raised Jesus the Nazarene through necromancy,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאן חֲשִׁיב בְּהָהוּא עָלְמָא?
phrases.english: He said to him: Who is important in that world?
He said to him: Israel.
Should I attach myself to them?
He said to him: Seek their welfare,
do not seek their harm,
anyone who touches them
is as if he touches the apple of His eye.
phrases.notes: זכריה 2:12

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the questions asked of בלעם, and the answer is the opposite of his.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Who is important in the next world, and should אונקלוס join them?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Israel; seek their good and not their harm.

steps.title: ישו's punishment
steps.stepSummary: אונקלוס asks ישו about his own punishment, and he answers: boiling excrement.
steps.simpleTranslation: He asked him: What is the punishment of 'that man'? He said: With boiling excrement.
steps.whatsHappening: As with בלעם, אונקלוס asks about the speaker's own punishment and gets an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer here is boiling excrement. The גמרא is about to explain in the next step which sin earns this punishment.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּינֵיהּ דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא בְּמַאי?
phrases.english: He said to him: The judgment of that man, with what is it?
He said to him: With boiling excrement.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּינֵיהּ דְּהָהוּא גַּבְרָא בְּמַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same conversation, now about ישו's own punishment.

steps.title: Source for the punishment of boiling excrement
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a teaching: anyone who mocks the words of the חכמים is sentenced to boiling excrement. This explains the punishment in the previous step.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the Master said: Anyone who mocks the words of the Sages is sentenced to boiling excrement.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the punishment from the last step by quoting a known teaching.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching connects boiling excrement to the sin of mocking the words of the חכמים. So the גמרא is telling us that this was ישו's sin: he mocked the words of the חכמים.

keyTerms.meaning: as the Master said (introduces a known teaching)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows how seriously חז"ל treat mocking the words of the חכמים: it is punished like this in the next world.

phrases.english: As the Master said:
Anyone who mocks the words of the Sages
is sentenced to boiling excrement.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source and reason for the punishment named in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: The punishment of boiling excrement in step 5.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A known teaching (דאמר מר): whoever mocks the words of the חכמים is sentenced to boiling excrement.

steps.title: The difference between Jewish sinners and the prophets of the nations
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sums up: look at the difference between the sinners of Israel and the prophets of the nations. בלעם, a prophet, wanted harm for Israel, while ישו, a Jewish sinner, wanted their good.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and see the difference between the sinners of Israel and the prophets of the nations of the world.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא steps out of the story to give its lesson from comparing the two answers.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם was a real prophet, and still he told אונקלוס not to seek Israel's good. ישו was a Jewish sinner, and still he told אונקלוס to seek Israel's good. The lesson: even a Jewish sinner keeps a loyalty to Israel that a non-Jewish prophet like בלעם did not have.

keyTerms.meaning: the prophets of the nations of the world

steps.whatToRemember: Three figures are raised, and each one's punishment fits his sin: טיטוס is burned and scattered, בלעם suffers in boiling semen, ישו suffers in boiling excrement for mocking the חכמים. בלעם and ישו both say Israel is most important in the next world, but only the Jewish sinner advises seeking Israel's good.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the lesson praises ישו. He is still punished severely. The point is only the contrast: even a Jewish sinner wished Israel well, while the prophet בלעם wished them harm.

phrases.english: Come and see what is the difference between
the sinners of Israel and the prophets of the nations of the world.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא חֲזִי מָה בֵּין פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לִנְבִיאֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from comparing בלעם's answer (step 2) with ישו's answer (step 4).
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even a sinner of Israel wished Israel well, while a prophet of the nations like בלעם wished them harm.

steps.title: The power of shame closes the בר קמצא story
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר teaches that shame is so powerful that הקב"ה helped בר קמצא, who had been humiliated, and destroyed His own בית המקדש.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches: רבי אלעזר said: Come and see how great the power of shame is. הקב"ה helped בר קמצא, and He destroyed His House and burned His Sanctuary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wraps up the long story of קמצא ובר קמצא with a closing lesson from a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בר קמצא was publicly humiliated, and that shame set off the chain of events that ended in the חורבן. רבי אלעזר reads this as God siding with the shamed person, even at the cost of the בית המקדש. The lesson is about how serious it is to embarrass someone.

keyTerms.meaning: It is taught in a ברייתא
Come and see. It introduces a lesson to notice
The Sanctuary, the main building of the בית המקדש

steps.whatToRemember: The story of בר קמצא ends with one message: embarrassing a person is so serious that it led to the חורבן.

phrases.english: It is taught: Rabbi Elazar says:

phrases.aramaic: בֹּא וּרְאֵה כַּמָּה גָּדוֹל(ה) כֹּחָהּ שֶׁל בּוּשָׁה,
phrases.english: Come and see how great is the power of shame,
phrases.notes: Some versions have the ה in round brackets, but the corrected wording leaves it out.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהֲרֵי סִיַּיע הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֶת בַּר קַמְצָא,
phrases.english: for the Holy One, Blessed be He, assisted bar Kamtza,
and He destroyed His House,
and burned His Sanctuary.

steps.triggerLanguage: תניא אמר רבי אלעזר בא וראה כמה גדול כחה של בושה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the קמצא ובר קמצא story and gives it a closing moral.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Shame is so powerful that God helped the humiliated בר קמצא, even to the point of destroying the בית המקדש.

steps.title: טור מלכא was destroyed over a rooster and a hen
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens a new story. טור מלכא was destroyed because of a rooster and a hen, and it starts by explaining the wedding custom behind it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of a rooster and a hen, טור מלכא was destroyed. Their custom was that when they led out a groom and bride, they carried a rooster and a hen in front of them, as if to say: be fruitful and multiply like chickens.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new story and sets up the background. It explains a wedding custom that will lead to the disaster.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The headline, a rooster and a hen, was mentioned earlier in the סוגיא. Now the גמרא fills in the details. The rooster and hen were a good-luck sign for having many children.

keyTerms.meaning: The King's Mountain, a Jewish area destroyed by the Romans

phrases.english: On account of a rooster and a hen, the King's Mountain was destroyed:
For they were accustomed
that when they would lead out a groom and bride,
they would take out before them a rooster and a hen,
as if to say: Be fruitful and multiply like chickens.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new story of destruction after the בר קמצא story closes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: טור מלכא's destruction began with the wedding custom of carrying a rooster and a hen.

steps.title: A small fight is reported as a revolt
steps.stepSummary: Roman soldiers took the chickens. The Jews beat the soldiers, who then told the קיסר that the Jews had rebelled, and the קיסר attacked.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day a troop of Romans passed by and took the chickens from them. The Jews fell on them and beat them. The soldiers went and told the קיסר: The Jews have rebelled against you! He came out against them.
steps.whatsHappening: The story moves forward. A small quarrel over chickens is reported to the קיסר as a rebellion, and war begins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is how a tiny incident grew into a full war. The soldiers' report turned a street fight into a revolt against the empire.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא חָלֵיף גּוּנְדָּא דְרוֹמָאֵי,
phrases.english: One day a troop of Romans was passing by,
and they took them from them.
phrases.notes: The soldiers took the rooster and the hen from the wedding party.

phrases.english: They fell upon them and beat them.
They came and said to the emperor:
The Jews have rebelled against you!
He came against them.

steps.triggerLanguage: יומא חד הוה קא חליף גונדא דרומאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the טור מלכא story with the event that set off the war.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The seized chickens led to a beating, a false report of rebellion, and war.

steps.title: בר דרומא fights and the קיסר prays
steps.stepSummary: A mighty warrior, בר דרומא, could leap a מיל and killed many Romans. The קיסר set his crown on the ground and begged God not to give him over to one man.
steps.simpleTranslation: Among the Jews was a man named בר דרומא, who could jump a מיל and kill Romans. The קיסר took off his crown and put it on the ground. He said: Master of the whole world, if it pleases You, do not hand over that man, him and his kingdom, into the hand of one man!
steps.whatsHappening: The story introduces a Jewish hero who was beating the Romans. The desperate קיסר prays to God, which sets up how בר דרומא will fall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בר דרומא was so strong that the קיסר felt helpless. The קיסר humbled himself by putting his crown on the ground and turning to God. That contrasts with what בר דרומא will say next.

keyTerms.meaning: A Jewish warrior of טור מלכא
A מיל, a measure of distance

phrases.english: There was among them a certain bar Deroma,
who would leap a mil and kill among them.
phrases.notes: A מיל is a distance a bit shorter than a mile, so this was a superhuman jump.

phrases.english: The emperor took his crown and placed it on the ground.
He said: Master of the entire world,
if it is pleasing to You,
do not hand over that man,
phrases.notes: "That man" is a polite way for the קיסר to talk about himself.

phrases.english: him and his kingdom,
into the hand of one man!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the war story with the Jewish hero and the קיסר's prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בר דרומא was defeating the Romans, and the humbled קיסר prayed for God's help.

steps.title: בר דרומא falls because of his own words
steps.stepSummary: בר דרומא was brought down by his own mouth. He quoted a פסוק as a complaint that God had abandoned Israel's armies.
steps.simpleTranslation: His mouth made בר דרומא stumble. He said: "Have You not, O God, rejected us, and You do not go out, O God, with our armies."
steps.whatsHappening: The story shows why בר דרומא fell. He spoke words against God, quoting a פסוק from תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בר דרומא said the פסוק as a statement of fact: God has rejected us and does not go out with our armies. Saying this caused his downfall. The next step asks how this can be a sin if דוד said the same words.

phrases.english: His mouth caused bar Deroma to stumble,
and he said: "Have You not, O God, rejected us,
phrases.notes: תהלים 60:12

phrases.english: and You go not forth, O God, with our armies."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason the hero lost, right after the קיסר's prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בר דרומא fell because he quoted a פסוק as a complaint that God had abandoned Israel.

steps.title: דוד said the same words
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: דוד המלך wrote the same פסוק, so why was it wrong for בר דרומא to say it?
steps.simpleTranslation: But דוד also said this!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a challenge. If these words appear in תהלים from דוד, how could saying them be a sin?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The attack is that the words cannot be bad in themselves, because they are part of תנ"ך. So something else must explain why בר דרומא was punished.

phrases.english: David also said this!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim in the previous step that saying this פסוק caused בר דרומא's fall.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that בר דרומא was punished for saying the פסוק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same words were said by דוד in תהלים, so the words alone cannot be sinful.

steps.title: דוד said it as a question
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that דוד said the words in wonder, as a question, while בר דרומא said them as a flat statement.
steps.simpleTranslation: דוד was saying it in wonder, as a question.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The difference is in how the words were said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דוד was asking God in pain: could it be that You have left us? בר דרומא stated as a fact that God had abandoned them. The same words can be a prayer or a denial, depending on the speaker's intent.

keyTerms.meaning: He was saying it in wonder, as a question

steps.whatToRemember: Same words, different meaning. דוד asked whether God had left them, which is a prayer. בר דרומא declared that God had left them, which brought his downfall.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying the פסוק itself is wrong to say. The problem was saying it as a statement of fact instead of as a question.

phrases.english: David was saying it in wonder, as a question.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the previous step.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes how the same words were said
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since דוד said these words, saying them could not be a sin.
steps.terutzMaskana: דוד said them as a question, while בר דרומא said them as a statement that God had left Israel, and that was his sin.

steps.title: בר דרומא dies and the emperor decides to leave
steps.stepSummary: בר דרומא goes into an outhouse, a snake kills him, and the קיסר sees this as a miracle and decides to leave the Jews alone this time.
steps.simpleTranslation: He went into the outhouse. A snake came, pulled out his intestines, and he died. The emperor said: Since a miracle was done for me, this time I will leave them alone. He left them alone and went away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the story of בר דרומא. After his words complaining that God had abandoned Israel (step 12), he dies suddenly, and the קיסר pulls back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man the קיסר was afraid of is killed without any Roman doing anything. The קיסר sees this as a miracle in his favor. Because of that, he chooses not to punish the Jews any further for now.

keyTerms.meaning: A miracle was done for me

phrases.english: He went into the outhouse,
a snake came and pulled out his intestines
and he died.
The emperor said: Since a miracle was done for me,
this time I will leave them alone.
He left them alone and went away.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the story after the side discussion about the פסוק in steps 13 and 14, and shows what happened to בר דרומא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בר דרומא died suddenly, and the קיסר took it as a miracle and withdrew.

steps.title: The Jews celebrate and the emperor comes back
steps.stepSummary: The Jews celebrate so brightly that the emperor feels mocked, and he returns to attack them.
steps.simpleTranslation: They jumped for joy, ate and drank, and lit so many lamps that the picture on a signet seal could be seen from a מיל away. The emperor said: The Jews are rejoicing over me! He came back and attacked them.
steps.whatsHappening: The Jews throw a huge celebration after the קיסר leaves. He sees it as them laughing at him, so he turns around and attacks again.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The danger had passed, but the celebration brought it back. The emperor reads their joy as joy over his own trouble, and that is what makes him return.

keyTerms.meaning: The picture or image stamped on the seal

phrases.english: They jumped for joy, ate and drank,
and lit lamps,
until the picture on a signet seal could be seen
from a mil away.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר: מִיחְדָּא קָא חָדוּ בִּי יְהוּדָאֵי!
phrases.english: He said: The Jews are rejoicing over me!
He came back and attacked them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story: the emperor's decision to leave is reversed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Jews' celebration made the emperor feel mocked, so he returned to attack.

steps.title: The massacre at the King's Mountain
steps.stepSummary: רבי אסי describes 300,000 swordsmen killing for three days in טור מלכא, while weddings went on at the other side, unaware.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אסי said: Three hundred thousand men with drawn swords entered the King's Mountain and killed there for three days and three nights. On the other side there were weddings and celebrations, and the two sides did not know about each other.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אסי adds a description of the attack itself. He stresses how huge the slaughter was and how huge the place was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The place was so large that a three-day massacre on one side was not heard about on the other side, where people were still celebrating. This sets up the next section about how big and crowded הר המלך was.

keyTerms.meaning: The King's Mountain, same as הַר הַמֶּלֶךְ

phrases.english: Rabbi Asi said:
Three hundred thousand men with drawn swords
entered the King's Mountain,

phrases.aramaic: וּקְטַלוּ בַּהּ תְּלָתָא יוֹמֵי וּתְלָתָא לֵילָווֹתָא;
phrases.english: and killed there for three days and three nights;
and on the other side there were weddings and celebrations,
and these did not know about those.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אַסִּי: תְּלָת מְאָה אַלְפֵי שְׁלִיפֵי סַיְיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Describes the attack that the emperor came back to carry out.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The slaughter at טור מלכא was huge, and the place was so vast that one side did not know about the other.

steps.title: The verse about God swallowing יעקב's dwellings
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן reads 'בלע ה׳ ולא חמל את כל נאות יעקב' as referring to the 600,000 cities of ינאי המלך on הר המלך.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'God swallowed up and did not pity all the dwellings of יעקב.' When רבין came, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: These are the six hundred thousand cities that ינאי המלך had on the King's Mountain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new piece. It brings a פסוק from איכה and explains which 'dwellings' were destroyed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks of 'all the dwellings of יעקב' in general. רבי יוחנן says it points to a specific place: the enormous number of cities of ינאי המלך on הר המלך.

keyTerms.meaning: The dwellings of יעקב (the Jewish people)
When רבין came (from ארץ ישראל to בבל)

phrases.english: "God swallowed up and did not pity
all the dwellings of Yaakov" –
phrases.notes: איכה 2:2

phrases.aramaic: כִּי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: When Ravin came, he said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
These are the six hundred thousand cities

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהָיוּ לוֹ לְיַנַּאי הַמֶּלֶךְ בְּהַר הַמֶּלֶךְ.
phrases.english: that King Yannai had on the King's Mountain.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּלַּע ה׳ וְלֹא חָמַל אֵת כׇּל נְאוֹת יַעֲקֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the mention of הר המלך by linking its destruction to a פסוק in איכה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: 'נאות יעקב' in the פסוק means the 600,000 cities of ינאי המלך on הר המלך.

steps.title: Backing for the six hundred thousand cities
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה, in the name of רב אסי, confirms the 600,000 cities and adds that each had as many people as left מצרים, and three had double.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יהודה said in the name of רב אסי: ינאי המלך had six hundred thousand cities on the King's Mountain. Each one had as many people as those who left מצרים, except for three, which had double that number.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another statement to support what רבי יוחנן said about the 600,000 cities.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'דאמר' ('as he said') shows this is backing for the previous step. It also adds new details: each city was as large as יוצאי מצרים, and three cities were twice as large. That sets up the next step, which names those three cities.

keyTerms.meaning: As he said; brings a supporting statement

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב אַסִּי:
phrases.english: As Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav Asi:

phrases.aramaic: שִׁשִּׁים רִבּוֹא עֲיָירוֹת הָיוּ לוֹ לְיַנַּאי הַמֶּלֶךְ
phrases.english: King Yannai had six hundred thousand cities
on the King's Mountain,

phrases.aramaic: וְכׇל אַחַת וְאַחַת הָיוּ בָּהּ כְּיוֹצְאֵי מִצְרַיִם,
phrases.english: and each and every one had as many people as those who left Egypt,
except for three
that had double the number of those who left Egypt.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב אַסִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבי יוחנן's claim of 600,000 cities and adds population details.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that ינאי המלך had 600,000 cities on הר המלך
steps.raayaSupportSource: A statement of רב יהודה in the name of רב אסי

steps.title: Naming the three largest cities
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא lists the three cities that had double the population of יוצאי מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: These are the three: כפר ביש, כפר שיחלים, and כפר דכריא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the three special cities from step 19. This sets up the next step, which explains each name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 19 mentioned three cities with double the population but did not name them. Here they are named, which leads directly into the explanation of the names.

keyTerms.meaning: These are they; introduces a list

phrases.english: These are they:

phrases.aramaic: כְּפַר בִּישׁ, כְּפַר שַׁיחֲלַיִים, כְּפַר דִּכְרַיָּא.
phrases.english: Kefar Bish, Kefar Shichalayim, Kefar Dichraya.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the three cities mentioned in step 19.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The three double-sized cities were כפר ביש, כפר שיחלים, and כפר דכריא.

steps.title: Why the three cities had those names
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains each name: כפר ביש did not host guests, כפר שיחלים lived from growing cress, and in כפר דכריא, as רבי יוחנן explains, women had boys first, then one girl, and stopped.
steps.simpleTranslation: כפר ביש was called that because they would not give a house to a guest. כפר שיחלים was called that because they made their living from cress. About כפר דכריא, רבי יוחנן said: Their wives would give birth to boys first, then give birth to a girl at the end, and then stop.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the meaning of each city's name, one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each name is tied to something true about that town. 'ביש' means bad, because the people refused guests. 'שיחלים' is cress, which they grew for a living. 'דכריא' comes from the word for male, because families there had mostly boys.

keyTerms.meaning: Cress, a plant grown for food

steps.whatToRemember: The destruction of הר המלך was beyond imagining. It had 600,000 cities, each as big as יוצאי מצרים, and the גמרא reads 'בלע ה׳ ולא חמל' in איכה as being about this place.

phrases.aramaic: כְּפַר בִּישׁ – דְּלָא יָהֲבִי בֵּיתָא לְאוּשְׁפִּיזָא.
phrases.english: Kefar Bish – because they would not give a house to a guest.
phrases.notes: בִּישׁ means 'bad', so the name means 'Bad Town'.

phrases.aramaic: כְּפַר שַׁיחֲלַיִים – שֶׁהָיְתָה פַּרְנָסָתָן מִן שַׁחֲלַיִים.
phrases.english: Kefar Shichalayim – because their living came from cress.
Kefar Dichraya – Rabbi Yochanan said:
phrases.notes: דִּכְרַיָּא comes from the word for 'male', so the name means 'Town of Males'.

phrases.english: that their wives would give birth to boys first,
and give birth to a girl at the end,
and then stop.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּפַר בִּישׁ – דְּלָא יָהֲבִי בֵּיתָא לְאוּשְׁפִּיזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the names listed in step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each city's name reflects its people: refusing guests, growing cress, and having mostly sons.

steps.title: עולא says the place is too small
steps.stepSummary: עולא reports that he saw הר המלך himself, and it could not even hold 600,000 reeds.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: I saw that place myself, and it could not even fit six hundred thousand reeds.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא raises a difficulty with the huge numbers from the previous steps. He saw the area himself, and it looks far too small.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 18-19 said there were 600,000 cities there, each as big as the population that left מצרים. עולא points out that the land today could not even hold 600,000 thin reeds, let alone that many cities. This sets up the challenge and the answer that follow.

keyTerms.meaning: six hundred thousand (sixty times ten thousand)

phrases.english: Ulla said:
I myself saw that place,
and even six hundred thousand reeds
it could not hold.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר עוּלָּא: לְדִידִי חֲזֵי לִי הָהוּא אַתְרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Raises an eyewitness difficulty against the population numbers given in steps 18-19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim of 600,000 cities on הר המלך, each as large as יוצאי מצרים.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The land is so small today that it could not even fit 600,000 reeds, so how could it hold that many cities?

steps.title: A heretic calls the Rabbis liars
steps.stepSummary: A מין tells רבי חנינא that these numbers are simply lies.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain heretic said to רבי חנינא: You are lying outright!
steps.whatsHappening: A מין takes the same difficulty and turns it into an attack. He says the חכמים are making things up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא only noticed the problem. The מין uses it to accuse the חכמים of exaggerating and lying. Now רבי חנינא needs to defend the claim.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא:
phrases.english: A certain heretic said to Rabbi Chanina:
You are lying outright!

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ הָהוּא מִינָא לְרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: שַׁקּוֹרֵי מְשַׁקְּרִיתוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Turns עולא's observation into an open accusation.
steps.kashyaTarget: The truth of the חכמים' description of the population.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Since the land is clearly too small, the claims must be false.

steps.title: The land stretches like a deer's skin
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא answers that ארץ ישראל is called ארץ צבי. Like a deer's skin, it expands when it is lived in and shrinks when it is empty.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The פסוק calls it "Land of the deer." A deer's skin cannot hold its flesh. In the same way, ארץ ישראל expands when people live on it and shrinks when no one lives on it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא answers the מין. He brings a פסוק showing that the land itself grows and shrinks.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The land looks small now because it is empty after the destruction. When it was full of Jews, it stretched to hold them all. So both things are true: the huge numbers then, and the small size עולא saw later.

keyTerms.meaning: land of the deer, a name for ארץ ישראל

steps.whatToRemember: ארץ ישראל expands when Jews live on it and shrinks when they don't. That is how the small area עולא saw could once have held such huge numbers.

phrases.english: He said to him:
"Land of the deer" is written about it,
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 3:19

phrases.english: just as this deer —
its skin cannot hold its flesh,
so too the Land of Israel —
when people live on it, it expands,
and when people do not live on it, it shrinks.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the מין's accusation and settles עולא's difficulty.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of reality based on a פסוק: the land's size changes.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The land's size is fixed, so the numbers must be exaggerated.
steps.terutzMaskana: The land expands when it is lived in, so in the days of the cities it was big enough.

steps.title: Three אמוראים ask for stories about כפר סכניא
steps.stepSummary: Three אמוראים sitting together ask whether anyone has heard something about כפר סכניא of מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מניומי בר חלקיה, רב חלקיה בר טוביה and רב הונא בר חייא were sitting together. They said: If anyone has heard something about כפר סכניא of מצרים, let him tell it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins here. Three אמוראים invite each other to share a story about a certain town. This is a setup line for the story that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nothing has been taught yet. The step only opens the floor. The answer comes in the next step, when one of them tells a story about a couple from that town.

phrases.english: Rav Minyumi bar Chilkiya
and Rav Chilkiya bar Toviya
and Rav Huna bar Chiyya
were sitting together,
they said:
If there is anyone who has heard something
about Kefar Sekhanya of Egypt,
let him say it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אִיכָּא דִּשְׁמִיעַ לֵיהּ מִילְּתָא מִכְּפַר סְכַנְיָא שֶׁל מִצְרַיִם, לֵימָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the size of the land to gathering a new story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Any story or teaching about כפר סכניא of מצרים.

steps.title: The captive couple who kept apart
steps.stepSummary: A betrothed couple were captured, and their captors married them to each other. She asked him not to touch her because she had no כתובה, and he never did, until the day he died.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of them said: There was a story with a betrothed man and woman who were captured by non-Jews, and the captors married them to each other. She said to him: Please do not touch me, because I have no כתובה from you. He did not touch her until the day he died.
steps.whatsHappening: One of the three answers the request with a story from כפר סכניא. The story is about a couple who held back, even though they were forced to live as husband and wife.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They were only ארוסים, so they were not yet allowed to live together. The non-Jews' marriage did not count, and she had no כתובה. So she asked him to keep away, and he listened for his whole life.

keyTerms.meaning: a betrothed man and his betrothed woman

phrases.english: One of them began and said:
There was a story with a betrothed man and his betrothed woman
who were taken captive among the non-Jews,
and they married them off to each other.
She said to him:
"Please, do not touch me,
for I have no marriage contract from you,"

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא נָגַע בָּהּ עַד יוֹם מוֹתוֹ.
phrases.english: and he did not touch her until the day of his death.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּתַח חַד מִינַּיְיהוּ וַאֲמַר: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאָרוּס וַאֲרוּסָתוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request from step 25 with a story.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A story of a betrothed couple from כפר סכניא who stayed apart for life because she had no כתובה.

steps.title: She praises him as greater than יוסף
steps.stepSummary: When he died, she told them to eulogize him, because his self-control was greater than יוסף's in three ways: every day instead of once, in one bed, and with his own wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he died, she said to them: Eulogize this man, who overcame his desire more than יוסף. יוסף faced it only for a short time, but this man faced it every day. יוסף was not in one bed with her, but this man was. And for יוסף she was not his wife, but here she was his wife.
steps.whatsHappening: The story ends with the woman's eulogy. She compares her husband to יוסף, who resisted אשת פוטיפר, and shows that her husband's test was harder.
steps.deeperAnalysis: She gives three points that make his test harder than יוסף's. It lasted his whole life, not one moment. He was right next to her. And she was already his wife through אירוסין, so the pull was even stronger.
steps.whatToRemember: This man's self-control is called greater than יוסף's: his test was daily, in one bed, and with his own wife.

phrases.english: And when he died, she said to them:
Eulogize this man,
who overcame his desire more than Yosef;
phrases.notes: She means יוסף resisting אשת פוטיפר, בראשית 39.

phrases.english: for with Yosef
it was only for one short time,
but this one, every single day.
And Yosef was not in one bed with her,
but this one was in one bed.
And for Yosef, she was not his wife,
but here, she was his wife.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story with the woman's eulogy and her comparison to יוסף.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The man's self-control was greater than יוסף's in three ways: it lasted every day, it was in one bed, and she was his own wife.

steps.title: The price of grain rose, and the town searched for the sin
steps.stepSummary: A second אמורא answers: the price of grain went up slightly. The town looked for a sin, found a father and son who sinned with a נערה מאורסה on יום הכיפורים, stoned them, and the price went back to normal.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another one began and said: Once forty measures of grain sold for one dinar. The price went up by one measure. They checked and found a father and son who had been with a betrothed girl on יום הכיפורים. They brought them to בית דין and stoned them, and the price went back to normal.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives his answer to the question from step 25 about כפר סכניא. He tells a story showing how seriously that town took sin.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a tiny change in the price of grain made the town ask what they had done wrong. They found the sinners and carried out the law, and the price recovered. The story shows a town that was very careful about justice.

keyTerms.meaning: Stoning, a death penalty of בית דין

phrases.english: Another one began and said:
It once happened that forty measures of grain stood at one dinar;
the rate dropped by one measure,
phrases.notes: Fewer measures for the same dinar means food got more expensive.

phrases.english: and they checked, and found a father and his son

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבָּאוּ עַל נַעֲרָה מְאוֹרָסָה בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים;
phrases.english: who had relations with a betrothed young woman on Yom Kippur;
and they brought them to court and stoned them,
and the rate returned to its place.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the question in step 25, after the first story in steps 26-27.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is known about כפר סכניא?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: It was a town so careful about sin that a small rise in price made them search out and punish sinners.

steps.title: A husband fakes his wife's adultery to avoid paying her כתובה
steps.stepSummary: A third אמורא tells of a man who wanted to divorce his wife without paying her large כתובה. He got his friends drunk, laid them in bed with her, put egg white there to look like semen, set up witnesses, and went to בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Another one began and said: There was a man who wanted to divorce his wife, but her כתובה was large. What did he do? He invited his friends, fed them and gave them drink, got them drunk, and laid them in one bed with her. He put egg white between them, set up witnesses, and went to בית דין.
steps.whatsHappening: A third אמורא starts another story about כפר סכניא. This step only sets up the trick; the next step tells how it was exposed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband wanted to make it look like his wife had been unfaithful, so that she would lose her כתובה. The egg white was meant to look like proof of relations. The story continues in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The marriage contract money owed to a wife if divorced

phrases.english: Another one began and said:
There was an incident with a certain man
who set his eyes on his wife to divorce her,
but her marriage contract was large.
What did he do?
He went and invited his friends
and fed them and gave them drink,
made them drunk and laid them on one bed,
phrases.notes: He laid his friends together with his wife in that bed.

phrases.english: and brought egg white and put it between them,
and set up witnesses over them,
and came to court.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּתַח אִידַּךְ וַאֲמַר: מַעֲשֶׂה בְּאָדָם אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third answer to the question in step 25, with a new story.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is known about כפר סכניא?
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A story of a husband's scheme against his wife, completed in the next step.

steps.title: בבא בן בוטא exposes the trick and the husband is punished
steps.stepSummary: בבא בן בוטא, a student of שמאי הזקן, shares a tradition: egg white hardens in fire, but semen does not. They tested it, found it was egg white, gave the husband lashes, and made him pay the full כתובה.
steps.simpleTranslation: There was an elder there, a student of שמאי הזקן, named בבא בן בוטא. He said: I have a tradition from שמאי הזקן that egg white hardens near fire, but semen dissolves near fire. They checked and found he was right. They brought the husband to בית דין, gave him lashes, and made him pay her כתובה.
steps.whatsHappening: The story from step 29 finishes. A wise elder uses a simple test to prove the husband lied.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The husband's whole case depended on the egg white looking like semen. A fire test showed what it really was, so the wife was cleared. The court punished the husband and made him pay the כתובה he tried to escape.

keyTerms.meaning: An elder, a student of שמאי הזקן
I have received as a tradition

phrases.english: There was a certain elder there
from the students of Shammai the Elder,
and Bava ben Buta was his name.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן, כָּךְ מְקוּבְּלַנִי מִשַּׁמַּאי הַזָּקֵן:
phrases.english: He said to them: This is what I received from Shammai the Elder:
egg white hardens from the fire,
but semen dissolves from the fire.
They checked and found it as he said,
and they brought him to court and gave him lashes,
and collected her marriage contract from him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָיָה שָׁם זָקֵן אֶחָד מִתַּלְמִידֵי שַׁמַּאי הַזָּקֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the story begun in step 29.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The husband's lie was exposed by a fire test, and he was punished and made to pay the כתובה.

steps.title: אביי asks why such a righteous town was punished
steps.stepSummary: אביי asks רב יוסף: if the people of this town were so righteous, why were they punished?
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said to רב יוסף: Since they were so righteous, why were they punished?
steps.whatsHappening: After hearing all these stories, אביי raises a difficulty. The stories show a righteous town, yet it was punished.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each story showed the town enforcing justice carefully. That seems to clash with the fact that the town suffered. אביי wants to know what sin could explain it.

phrases.english: Abaye said to Rav Yosef:
But since they were so righteous,
what is the reason they were punished?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמֵאַחַר דַּהֲווֹ צַדִּיקִים כּוּלֵּי הַאי, מַאי טַעְמָא אִיעֲנוּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reacts to all the stories about כפר סכניא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The fact that כפר סכניא was punished.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The stories show the town was very righteous, so their punishment seems unexplained.

steps.title: They were punished for not mourning ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף answers that they did not mourn for ירושלים, and brings a פסוק showing that only those who mourn for ירושלים will rejoice with her.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: Because they did not mourn for ירושלים, as it is written: "Rejoice with ירושלים and be glad with her, all who love her; rejoice greatly with her, all who mourn for her."
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף answers אביי's question. Their sin was not mourning the loss of ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The town did well in its own justice, but it lacked feeling for ירושלים. The פסוק promises joy to those who mourn for her, which implies that those who do not mourn lose that share.
steps.whatToRemember: Even a town careful about justice was punished because it did not mourn for ירושלים. Mourning for ירושלים is what earns a share in her joy.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the idea that whoever mourns for ירושלים will see her joy.

phrases.english: He said to him:
Because they did not mourn for Jerusalem,
as it is written:

phrases.aramaic: ״שִׂמְחוּ אֶת יְרוּשָׁלִַם וְגִילוּ בָהּ כׇּל אוֹהֲבֶיהָ,
phrases.english: "Rejoice with Jerusalem and be glad with her, all who love her,
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 66:10

phrases.aramaic: שִׂישׂוּ אִתָּהּ מָשׂוֹשׂ כׇּל הַמִּתְאַבְּלִים עָלֶיהָ״.
phrases.english: rejoice greatly with her, all who mourn for her."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers אביי's question in step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Identifies a hidden sin that explains the punishment.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A town so careful about justice should not have been punished.
steps.terutzMaskana: Their failure to mourn for ירושלים caused the punishment, based on the פסוק in ישעיהו.

steps.title: The custom of planting trees for newborns in ביתר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the line 'because of a carriage shaft, ביתר was destroyed.' It first describes a local custom: a cedar was planted for each baby boy and a cypress for each baby girl. When they married, the trees were cut down to build their חופה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of a carriage shaft, ביתר was destroyed. In ביתר they had a custom: when a boy was born, they planted a cedar tree. When a girl was born, they planted a cypress. When the two later married, they cut down those trees and used them to make the wedding canopy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the third line of the earlier list and begins to explain it. This step sets up the background custom that the story depends on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the story can make sense, we need to know why one cut-down tree mattered so much. These trees were tied to each child's future wedding, so the people of ביתר treated them as very precious.

keyTerms.meaning: ביתר, a large Jewish city destroyed by the Romans

phrases.english: Because of a carriage shaft, Beitar was destroyed:
For they were accustomed:

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֲוָה מִתְיְלִיד יָנוֹקָא – שָׁתְלִי אַרְזָא,
phrases.english: when a boy was born, they would plant a cedar;
for a girl, they would plant a cypress.
And when they would get married,
they would cut them down and make a wedding canopy.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After finishing the טור מלכא material and the stories about כפר סכניא (closed by רב יוסף's answer to אביי), the גמרא turns to the third item in the earlier list: ביתר.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ביתר's custom of planting a cedar or cypress for each newborn, later used for the חופה, is the background to its destruction.

steps.title: The broken carriage and the false report of rebellion
steps.stepSummary: The emperor's daughter's carriage shaft broke, and her servants cut down one of the special cedars to fix it. The people of ביתר beat the servants, who then told the קיסר that the Jews had rebelled, and he went to war against them.
steps.simpleTranslation: One day the emperor's daughter was passing through, and the pole of her carriage broke. Her servants cut down a cedar and brought it to her. The Jews came and attacked them and beat them. The servants went and told the emperor: 'The Jews have rebelled against you!' So the emperor came to fight against them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the story and shows how one cut-down tree led to war against ביתר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The servants took a cedar from the trees in step 33, so the people of ביתר felt something precious had been stolen. Their angry reaction was reported to the קיסר as a rebellion, and that turned a small fight into a war.

phrases.aramaic: יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא חָלְפָא בְּרַתֵּיה דְּקֵיסָר,
phrases.english: One day the emperor's daughter was passing by;
the shaft of the carriage broke.
They cut down a cedar and brought it to her.
phrases.notes: "They" here means her servants, and the cedar was one of the special wedding trees.

phrases.english: They came, fell upon them, and beat them.
phrases.notes: Now "they" means the people of ביתר, and they beat the servants.

phrases.english: They came and said to the emperor:
The Jews have rebelled against you!
He came against them.

steps.triggerLanguage: יוֹמָא חַד הֲוָה קָא חָלְפָא בְּרַתֵּיה דְּקֵיסָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ביתר story using the custom described in step 33.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A cut-down cedar led to a beating, which was falsely reported as rebellion, and that brought the קיסר to war against ביתר.
steps.whatToRemember: ביתר's destruction started from something small: one tree cut down for a broken carriage pole, and a report that called the angry reaction a rebellion.

steps.title: Eighty thousand battle trumpets and blood reaching the sea
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא, quoting רבי אבהו, quoting רבי יוחנן, reads the פסוק 'He cut off all the horn of Israel' as being about the 80,000 soldiers with battle trumpets who entered ביתר. They killed so many people that the blood flowed all the way to the Mediterranean Sea, even though the city was a מיל away.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'He cut off in His fierce anger all the horn of Israel.' רבי זירא said in the name of רבי אבהו, who said in the name of רבי יוחנן: these are the eighty thousand battle trumpets that entered the city of ביתר when it was captured. They killed men, women and children there, until the blood flowed and poured into the Great Sea. In case you think the city was close to the sea, it was a מיל away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק from איכה and רבי יוחנן's explanation to show how huge the killing in ביתר was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'horn' in the פסוק is read as war trumpets, meaning a huge army that entered the city. The extra line about the distance blocks an easy answer: the blood did not just run into a nearby sea, it flowed a whole מיל.

keyTerms.meaning: battle horns or trumpets, standing for soldiers
a measure of distance, about one kilometer

phrases.english: "He has cut off in fierce anger all the horn of Israel":
phrases.notes: איכה 2:3

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said that Rabbi Abbahu said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
These are the eighty thousand battle trumpets
phrases.notes: The word in square brackets, אלף, is added in the corrected wording.

phrases.english: that entered the city of Beitar when they captured it,
and they killed men, women, and children there,

phrases.aramaic: עַד שֶׁהָלַךְ דָּמָן וְנָפַל לַיָּם הַגָּדוֹל.
phrases.english: until their blood flowed and fell into the Great Sea.
Perhaps you will say it was close?
It was a mil away.

steps.triggerLanguage: גָּדַע בׇּחֳרִי אַף כֹּל קֶרֶן יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the war began in step 34, the גמרא describes how terrible the slaughter was, using a פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 'horn of Israel' in איכה refers to the 80,000 trumpet-bearing soldiers who captured ביתר, and the blood flowed a מיל to the sea.

steps.title: Rivers that were one-third blood
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא quotes רבי אליעזר הגדול: two rivers in בקעת ידים flowed in opposite directions, and the חכמים estimated they were two parts water and one part blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches that רבי אליעזר הגדול says: there are two rivers in the valley of ידים. One flows one way and the other flows the other way. The חכמים estimated that they held two parts water and one part blood.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports how huge the bloodshed was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 35 said the blood reached the sea. This ברייתא adds another picture: whole rivers were made up of one-third blood, so the killing really was enormous.

keyTerms.meaning: it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: It was taught: Rabbi Eliezer the Great says:
There are two rivers in the Valley of Yadayim,

phrases.aramaic: אֶחָד מוֹשֵׁךְ אֵילָךְ, וְאֶחָד מוֹשֵׁךְ אֵילָךְ,
phrases.english: one flowing this way and one flowing that way,
and the Sages estimated
two parts water and one part blood.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a ברייתא that supports the huge amount of blood described by רבי יוחנן.
steps.raayaObject: That the bloodshed at ביתר was enormous
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא of רבי אליעזר הגדול about two rivers that were one-third blood

steps.title: Seven years of vineyards fertilized with blood
steps.stepSummary: Another ברייתא teaches that for seven years, non-Jews harvested their vineyards without using fertilizer, because the soil was soaked with Jewish blood.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: for seven years the non-Jews harvested their vineyards without fertilizer, because of the blood of the Jewish people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings one more ברייתא to show how much Jewish blood was spilled in ביתר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rivers showed blood in the water. Now the ground itself was so full of blood that it fed the vineyards for seven years, so no fertilizer was needed.

keyTerms.meaning: it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita:

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁבַע שָׁנִים בָּצְרוּ גּוֹיִם אֶת כַּרְמֵיהֶן
phrases.english: For seven years the gentiles harvested their vineyards
from the blood of Israel, without fertilizer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second ברייתא that adds to the picture from step 36.
steps.raayaObject: That the bloodshed at ביתר was enormous
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא saying the vineyards needed no fertilizer for seven years
steps.whatToRemember: The ביתר section shows a small event, one cut-down cedar, leading to massive destruction. The blood reached the sea a מיל away, filled rivers, and fed vineyards for seven years.
